summary: Explains which parts of IPv6 matter for second and third generation cellular hosts, and how to use them given limited bandwidth, cost and delay on cellular links. It gives guidance to implementers of such devices. It was replaced by RFC 7066.

eli5.summary: Phones on slow, pricey connections cannot use every feature of the new internet addressing. This document says which parts a phone really needs and how to use them sensibly.

subtitle: Which IPv6 features mobile phones on slow networks actually need.

tldr.problem: Mobile phones on 2G and 3G networks (GPRS, UMTS) have limited bandwidth and expensive data, but IPv6 covers many features and specifications. Implementers need guidance on which parts are essential.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists IPv6 specifications relevant to cellular hosts and discusses which are mandatory, optional, or not needed for these devices, considering bandwidth and cost constraints.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 7066 with updated guidance for modern cellular networks.

today: RFC 3316 is Informational and has been superseded by RFC 7066, which provides updated guidance for IPv6 in cellular networks including evolved standards and modern device capabilities. The core principles of selective IPv6 implementation remain relevant for resource-constrained devices.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Second and third generation cellular technologies (GPRS, UMTS, CDMA2000) enable mobile phones to connect to the Internet continuously. IPv6 support is becoming mandatory in cellular standards because IPv4 addresses will run out. The challenge is deciding which parts of IPv6 to implement on phones with limited bandwidth, power and cost constraints. This document guides implementers on the essential IPv6 features for cellular hosts.
sections.eli5: Mobile phones need new internet addresses (IPv6), but they cannot use every feature because phones have slow connections and limited data plans. This explains what is actually needed.

sections.title: Basic IP Core Features
sections.content: Cellular hosts must implement the fundamental IPv6 specifications: the base IPv6 protocol, Neighbor Discovery, stateless address autoconfiguration, and ICMPv6. Path MTU Discovery is optional but recommended to use bandwidth efficiently. Address resolution and duplicate detection are simplified in cellular networks because the phone connects via a point-to-point link to a single gateway router (the GGSN). Multicast Listener Discovery is required for multicast group knowledge. DNS should be supported, preferably with recursive mode to reduce signaling over the air interface.
sections.eli5: Core internet features like finding the path to send packets, learning your own address, and handling error messages are required. Some features used in traditional networks are simpler or skipped because the phone talks directly to one gateway.

sections.title: IP Security (IPsec)
sections.content: IPsec (both AH and ESP headers) is mandatory in IPv6. Cellular hosts must support key IPsec algorithms including HMAC-MD5, HMAC-SHA, AES-based encryption, and the NULL encryption algorithm. Automatic key management via IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is not always practical for cellular devices because phone addresses change when moving networks. Some applications (like IMS) may use alternative key management, such as UMTS AKA (Authentication and Key Agreement). The interaction between ICMPv6 and IPsec policies requires careful handling to avoid deadlocks during security association negotiation.
sections.eli5: Phones can encrypt and protect their data, but setting up these protections is tricky because phone addresses change frequently. Some features and workarounds are described.

sections.title: Addressing and Configuration
sections.content: Cellular hosts must support IPv6 Addressing Architecture and stateless address autoconfiguration as defined in RFC 2462. In 3GPP networks, the Gateway GPRS Support Node (GGSN) assigns a unique prefix to each phone, eliminating the need for duplicate address detection. Privacy Extensions (RFC 3041) are optional but useful for temporary addresses. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) may be used for configuration beyond address assignment. Default Address Selection (RFC 3484) is needed to handle multiple addresses correctly. IPv6 over PPP is mandatory for phones implementing PPP to enable PC cards or tethering.
sections.eli5: The phone gets an address automatically when it connects. Different configuration methods exist, and the phone can use temporary addresses for privacy.

sections.title: 3GPP Network Model
sections.content: The 3GPP model uses a point-to-point architecture where each phone connects directly to a gateway router. The GGSN provides each phone with a unique prefix and an interface identifier, avoiding conflicts. Duplicate address detection (DAD) is not needed over the air because the GGSN ensures prefix uniqueness. This efficient design allows phones to implement stateless autoconfiguration without the overhead of duplicate detection. The phone can use multiple prefixes and implement privacy extensions without additional DAD messages, conserving bandwidth and battery power.
sections.eli5: The phone's connection to the network is direct and simple, so complicated address checks are not needed. This saves power and bandwidth.
